Paragraph:
Translation: A self-realized man has no purpose to fulfill in the discharge of his prescribed duties, nor has he any reason not to perform such work. Nor has he any need to depend on any other living being.

Purport (Excerpt): A self-realized man is no longer obliged to perform any prescribed duty, save and except activities in Krsna consciousness. Krsna consciousness is not inactivity either... A Krsna conscious man does not take shelter of any person—man or demigod.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Understanding the complete psychological and spiritual freedom of a realized person regarding gain, loss, and dependency.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna explains that a self-realized person has nothing to gain by doing work and nothing to lose by not doing work, nor do they rely on anyone for their well-being. Yet, they do not default to apathy.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna understands that true spiritual freedom removes personal ulterior motives from action while preserving freedom of movement.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Autonomy: Operating with self-governance and freedom from external reliance
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Freedom from Outcome Dependence: Acting without being driven by fear of loss or craving for personal gain
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Unconditional Action: Engaging in life without transactional motives

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Nartha-krtanarthena (No selfish gain from performing work, nor harm from omitting it)
Sarva-bhutesu kascid artha-vyapasrayah (No reliance on any entity for self-interest)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: A self-realized soul operates beyond selfish incentives. They gain no personal benefit from working, suffer no loss by refraining, and depend on no creation for their security, acting in complete spiritual liberty.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: When you act without transactional motives or fear, your actions become genuine and stress-free. Real freedom is being able to engage with the world without needing it to deliver your self-worth or happiness.
